title: One group, three companies: who you sign with
excerpt: Aapastech runs through Aapastech Private Limited in India, Aapastech OÜ in the EU and UK, and 14818032 Canada Inc. elsewhere. Here is why and what it means for you.
content:
Why not one company?

We started in Delhi in 2022, and Aapastech Private Limited was the natural home for the work. Then customers arrived from Europe and North America, and each brought its own expectations: an invoice from a company in their market, a contract under a law their lawyers know, and a data controller they can actually reach.

You can sell into the EU from an Indian company. Plenty of firms do. But a German retailer's procurement team asks harder questions when the controller of its customers' data sits outside the EU, and a Canadian buyer wants to know which courts apply if something goes wrong. Answering those questions one deal at a time slows every deal down.

How it works

  • India: Aapastech Private Limited, Delhi. Indian law, courts at Delhi. Data fiduciary under Indian law.
  • European Union and United Kingdom: Aapastech OÜ, Tallinn. Estonian law, Harju County Court, and GDPR controller.
  • Everywhere else: 14818032 Canada Inc., Ontario. Ontario law and the courts of Ontario.

For a business, the company you deal with follows the country of your billing address. Each company bills and collects payment from its own customers. The three share one engineering team, one hosting setup and one support desk, and each processes data for the others under a written intra-group agreement.

What stays the same

The products and services. Tyashin, Thridify, YOM and the rest work the same way for a customer in Pune, Porto or Phoenix. Your prices show in your currency and your legal pages name your company, and that is the whole difference.

What this site does with it

When you open aapastech.com we read the country your connection comes from and show the company, prices and legal terms for that region. If we guessed wrong, because you use a VPN or you are travelling, pick your region from the switcher in the footer and we will remember it. You can see all three companies on our About page.

title: How our Grievance Officer handles a complaint
excerpt: Acknowledged in 24 hours, resolved in 7 days, harmful content down in 36 hours or 2. The clocks behind our grievance process under India’s IT Rules.
content:
Tyashin hosts websites and Thridify hosts 3D models and product pages for other businesses. Under India's Information Technology Rules that makes them intermediaries, and an intermediary has to name a Grievance Officer and answer complaints on a fixed clock. The rules were tightened again in February 2026, so here is how we run it.

One officer, one inbox

Every complaint about any of our products goes to the same person and the same address. That covers content on a site we host, how we handle someone's personal data, or the service itself. Anyone can complain, whether they have an account or not. One inbox means nothing falls between brands.

The clocks

  • 24 hours to acknowledge a complaint and give a reference number.
  • 7 days to resolve it.
  • 36 hours to act on a request to remove hosted content that breaks our user rules. Ownership and intellectual property disputes can take up to 7 days, because both sides have to be heard.
  • 2 hours to remove or block content that shows someone in a private or sexual way, or impersonates them, including images changed with AI.
  • One month to answer requests to see, correct or delete personal data.

What we changed to meet them

The 2-hour clock is the hard one. It does not wait for business hours, so takedown cannot depend on one person being awake. We wrote an incident and takedown runbook that says who can disable a hosted page, how evidence is preserved, and how the customer is told. The footers of Tyashin, Thridify and YOM link to the grievance page, which is also published in Hindi.

If the answer is not good enough

A complainant who disagrees with our decision can appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee at gac.gov.in within 30 days. People in the EU, the UK and Canada have their own regulators, listed on our Grievance Officer page.

title: How we label AI images across our products
excerpt: India’s 2026 IT Rules and Article 50 of the EU AI Act both ask for AI images to be marked. What we label, how we keep C2PA credentials, and our deadlines.
content:
Several of our products make images with AI. Tyashin for LinkedIn creates post illustrations, Tyashin's blog tools create article images, and Thridify can render product scenes. Two sets of rules now say those images must be marked as AI-made, and they arrive within a month of each other.

The two rules

  • India's IT Rules, as amended in February 2026, ask intermediaries that offer AI tools to label synthetic content and attach metadata that identifies it. We are working to a 31 December 2026 deadline.
  • Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act requires providers of AI systems that generate images to mark them in a machine-readable way. That applies from 2 December 2026.

What we label

Every AI image our products create carries a visible label where it is shown and machine-readable metadata in the file. Tyashin for LinkedIn has done this since 28 October 2026. Tyashin and Thridify follow before the deadlines above. We only use image models that mark their own output.

Why we keep C2PA credentials intact

Models from OpenAI and Google attach C2PA content credentials, a signed record of how the image was made. It is easy to destroy them by accident: resizing or converting an image the wrong way strips them. We are changing our image pipelines so they keep those credentials and add our own metadata alongside, instead of rewriting the file. We are also working toward membership of the Content Authenticity Initiative, the group behind the standard.

Chatbots too

Article 50(1) covers conversation as well. The Tyashin chatbot now tells visitors they are talking to an AI before anything else. You can follow the status of each of these on our trust page.

title: What being registered with CERT-In means for our customers
excerpt: We gave CERT-In a point of contact on 27 October 2026. What that commits us to: incident reports within 6 hours, 180-day logs and synced clocks.
content:
CERT-In is India's national computer emergency response team. Its 2022 directions apply to any company that runs systems in India or serves Indian users, and they start with a simple requirement: give CERT-In a named point of contact. We sent ours on 27 October 2026 for Aapastech Private Limited and 14818032 Canada Inc.

What the directions ask

  • Report certain cyber incidents to CERT-In within 6 hours of noticing them.
  • Keep logs of our systems for 180 days, in India, and hand them over when CERT-In asks.
  • Sync every system clock to a trusted time source, so logs from different systems line up.
  • Answer CERT-In's requests through the named contact.

Where we are

Our Google Cloud systems already keep logs for 180 days. We have prepared storage for Cloudflare logs and are switching on the remaining log feeds, with 31 December 2026 as our deadline. The incident runbook that covers the 6-hour report is written.

Why customers should care

If something goes wrong, a company with a named contact, kept logs and a rehearsed process can find out what happened and fix it. That protects the businesses that run on Tyashin, Thridify and YOM, and their customers. See the current status on our trust page.
